title: Mara defeated
hook: the army scatters; a voice from the sky tells Mara to give up (Buddhacarita 13)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mara comes, and your line: the bow of flowers. Did you notice a soft pull and give it a breath? Today the army attacks. Day seven hundred sixteen.

The army doesn't stop to talk. Mara has already tried talking: a speech about duty, a flower arrow, and the man under the tree didn't stir. So now everything the army can lift, it throws. Rocks, trees, spears, fire. The air around the tree fills with howling and smoke. In the middle of it, one man sits with his legs crossed and his eyes steady. He doesn't answer. He doesn't flinch. And then a voice speaks from somewhere above the noise, from someone nobody can see.
screen: `ROCKS, TREES, SPEARS, FIRE.` → `ONE MAN, SITTING STILL.` → `A VOICE FROM ABOVE.`

segments.voice: First, the attack. The poem gives the army full force. Some hurl boulders. Some swing whole trees. Some throw weapons, some breathe fire, some try to terrify him with shrieks and faces. Second, what happens to it. Nothing lands. In the poem, paraphrased here, what's thrown at him stops in the air, or falls short, or turns harmless. The fire doesn't burn him. The noise doesn't move him. Weapons that would break anyone else fail on this one seated man. Third, the voice. Then a being in the sky, unseen, speaks to Mara. Give up this useless effort, it says. Lay down your anger. You can no more shake this man than the wind can shake the great mountain. Fire might lose its heat, water its wetness, the earth its firmness, before he gives up his resolve. He has made his vow, and the time has come for it to be fulfilled. Fourth, the scattering. Mara hears it. He looks at the man under the tree, still unmoved. And the poem says he goes away disheartened, his effort spent, and his army scatters in every direction. The sky clears. Flowers fall from it. Look at how the victory is won. The prince never lifts a hand. He never argues back, never calls for help, never fights. The poem doesn't even give him a line. His whole answer to the army is to keep sitting. And the army, which could break anything that resisted, has nothing to push against. What scatters it isn't a stronger army. It's stillness that won't be moved. Tomorrow the night goes on, and the poem turns from what he refused to what he sees.
screen: `THE ARMY THROWS EVERYTHING.` · `NOTHING LANDS.` · `NO WIND SHAKES THE MOUNTAIN.` · `MARA GOES, DISHEARTENED.` · then, large: `THE ARMY SCATTERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one fear pass. Settle, and breathe. Bring back the fear you named yesterday, or another that's here today. Let it come close. Don't push it away and don't follow it. Just keep sitting, the way the prince keeps sitting while the army howls. Feel the breath come in and go out underneath it. Watch the fear rise, peak, and begin to thin. If it doesn't thin, that's all right. Let it stay, and keep breathing. Fears, like armies, sometimes run out of things to throw. The bell holds the time.
Mara defeated. The army throws everything at the seated prince and nothing lands; a voice from the sky tells Mara to give up, and his army scatters. Today's word.
Your line: the army scatters. Today, when something comes at you loud and fast, try not answering for one breath, and see what's left of it when the noise stops. Day seven hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Buddhist art shows the Buddha seated at the moment of victory over Mara, and in some traditions the story is retold at festivals of the awakening.

fork.setup: you're Mara. your flower arrow failed, and now your whole army has failed too. a voice from the sky tells you to give up. what do you do?
options: sit down beside him and learn.
fork.reveal: Mara looks once more at the unmoved man and goes away disheartened. his army scatters, the sky clears, and flowers fall.

original.note: Sanskrit: unmoving, steady; also a word for a mountain.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha defeated Mara in a battle.
what it means: in the poem he never fights; the army's weapons fail, a voice tells Mara to stop, and Mara leaves.
what a scholar hears: Ashvaghosha gives the victory no speech from the prince at all, so his steadiness is the whole answer, likened to a mountain no wind can move.

sources.ref: Buddhacarita 13 (the army's attack, the voice from the sky, Mara's departure)

notes: All Buddhacarita material paraphrased (Cowell 1894 is not on the validator list).

Confirm in Cowell canto 13: what happens to the weapons (stopping in the air, falling short, fire not burning, missiles turning harmless); the unseen being in the sky telling Mara to cease his vain effort, with the comparisons (wind and Mount Meru; fire losing heat, water its wetness, earth its firmness); Mara departing dejected, his army scattering, the sky clearing and flowers falling.

The script says the prince has no line in this scene; confirm that canto 13 gives him no speech to Mara. Later tellings add the earth-touching gesture and the earth as witness; this script leaves them out because the outline cites canto 13 only.
howItsDone: Buddhist art of the victory over Mara (often the earth-touching posture, not mentioned in the script); confirm. Festival retellings: confirm.
Original: acala as 'mountain' is a standard dictionary sense; confirm.
Editor: hook reworked: 'as he sat yesterday' / 'Tonight' wrongly put the attack on a later night (the poem keeps it one night), and the fragment-list opener repeated day 715's shape.
Auditor: deep-read against Buddhacarita (Cowell) and days 697-716; no change needed.
